opus-5.5.text:
Mathematics is attractive for a few reasons. The most important is verifiability. In many research domains, it's hard to tell whether a contribution is good. You might have to run expensive experiments, wait years for results to replicate, or rely on noisy expert judgment. In math, if a model claims to have solved a problem, you can check the answer. For well-posed problems with definite numerical or symbolic answers, you can grade automatically. As formal proof assistants like Lean mature, you can increasingly verify proofs mechanically too. That gives you a clean, objective signal, which is rare when you're trying to measure something as fuzzy as research ability.

The second reason is that math is a good proxy for the kinds of reasoning we care about in research generally. Solving a hard problem means understanding what's known, finding the right abstractions, connecting ideas from different areas, and carrying out long chains of reasoning without making errors. Those are core skills in science and engineering. If a system can do genuinely novel mathematical work, that tells you something meaningful about its capacity for open-ended intellectual work.

Third, math has a smooth difficulty gradient. You can go from high school competition problems to olympiad problems to research-level questions that would take a professional mathematician hours or days, all the way up to open problems. That lets you track progress over time rather than having a benchmark that is saturated almost immediately or that nothing can touch.

It's also relatively self-contained. You don't need lab equipment or access to the physical world. Everything happens in the space of ideas, so it isolates the reasoning component from bottlenecks like experimentation or data collection.

That said, I'd be careful about over-interpreting results. Math is unusually well-suited to verification, and that's partly why AI might progress faster there than in messier domains. Strong math performance doesn't automatically mean a system can do good research in biology or economics, where problems are less well-defined and feedback is slower and noisier. So I think of math as a useful leading indicator and a clean testbed, not a complete picture of research capability.

r001.rationale: The response presents math as a testbed with automatically checkable answers and describes the long chains of reasoning needed for hard research problems.

r002.rationale: It describes connecting ideas from different areas as a core reasoning skill and says novel mathematical work can reveal AI’s capacity for open-ended intellectual work.

r003.rationale: The response does not say AI has made comparatively little progress in creatively combining ideas to produce scientific insights.

fable-5.1.text:
Mathematics is appealing for a few reasons. The first is that it's a domain where verification is relatively cheap and relatively unambiguous. If a model produces a proof, you can check whether the proof is correct, and in the limit you can formalize it in something like Lean and have a machine check it. That's very different from most of science or engineering, where evaluating a research contribution requires expensive experiments, long feedback loops, or a lot of expert judgment that people disagree about. So math lets you isolate the question "can this system do genuinely hard intellectual work?" from the question "can we even tell?"

The second reason is that mathematics has a very wide range of difficulty, and that range is legible. You have competition problems at the bottom, which are hard but ultimately closed-form and solvable in hours. Then you have problems that a strong graduate student might spend weeks on, and then open problems that research mathematicians have been stuck on for years or decades. That gives you a ladder, and you can ask where on the ladder current systems fall and how fast they're climbing. With benchmarks like FrontierMath, part of the motivation was precisely that the existing math benchmarks had saturated, and we wanted problems where the gap between "model solves this" and "this is research-level work" was much smaller.

The third thing, and this is maybe the most important from my perspective, is that mathematics is a reasonable proxy for a lot of what AI research itself involves. Not all of it, obviously, since running experiments and managing compute and taste about which directions matter are their own skills. But the core of it is long chains of reasoning, holding a complicated structure in your head, noticing when an approach isn't working and backtracking, and generating ideas that aren't just interpolations of things you've seen before. If models can't do that in math, where the environment is clean, it's unlikely they can do it in messier domains. And conversely, if they start doing it in math, that's an early signal that the capabilities relevant to automating research are arriving.

I'd add one caveat, which is that math can also mislead you if you're not careful. It's possible to get very good at a certain style of problem through training on a lot of similar material without that generalizing to open-ended research. So you want to be attentive to whether the problems are genuinely novel and whether the model is doing something that looks like discovery rather than retrieval. That's part of why we care about problems that are unpublished and that working mathematicians consider hard.

r001.rationale: The response describes long chains of reasoning in mathematics and says proofs can be checked automatically with tools such as Lean.

r002.rationale: It mentions generating ideas beyond interpolation, but does not specifically express interest in testing whether AI can creatively connect disparate mathematical ideas.

r003.rationale: It cautions that models may rely on similar training material, but does not judge that AI has shown comparatively little progress in creatively combining ideas to produce scientific insights.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematics is useful because it combines problems that require real creativity with a relatively clear way of checking whether you’ve succeeded. In many other areas of research, evaluating an idea might require running an expensive experiment, or waiting a long time to see whether a prediction holds up. In mathematics, if you produce a proof, you can scrutinize that proof—and, if it’s formalized, use a proof checker to verify it.

That lets us separate generating an insight from checking it. The checking can be quite reliable even when finding the solution is very difficult. And there’s a broad range of difficulty, from problems we know how to solve to open questions that would represent genuine research progress.

The caveat is that solving a well-specified problem isn’t the whole of research. You also have to choose worthwhile questions, develop useful concepts, and recognize which directions are promising. So mathematics gives us a tractable setting for testing some important parts of research ability, without assuming that success there automatically transfers to every scientific field.

r001.rationale: The response describes proof checking, including formal proof checkers, but does not identify long-horizon research reasoning as the target.

r002.rationale: It says mathematical problems require creativity, but does not discuss AI connecting disparate mathematical ideas.

r003.rationale: It does not assess AI’s progress, comparatively or otherwise, in creatively combining ideas to produce scientific insights.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematics is useful because it combines problems that are very easy to state with problems that require genuinely new ideas to solve. And there’s a fairly clear way to check whether you’ve succeeded: you can examine the proof, or, in some settings, verify it formally. That makes it easier to distinguish a plausible-sounding answer from an actual contribution.

It also captures quite a lot of what makes research difficult. You have to choose promising directions, come up with useful intermediate results, notice when an approach isn’t working, and sometimes introduce a new abstraction. So you can test more than whether a model knows facts or can reproduce a familiar solution. You can ask whether it can make progress on something it hasn’t seen before.

Of course, it’s a sandbox. It doesn’t capture everything about empirical science, like designing experiments or dealing with messy measurements. But it gives us a relatively clean setting in which to study some of the abilities that might underpin more general AI research.

r001.rationale: It describes mathematics as a sandbox for testing research abilities such as choosing directions, developing intermediate results, and making progress on unfamiliar problems, with proofs or formal verification providing a clear way to check results.

r002.rationale: It mentions introducing abstractions and making progress on unfamiliar problems, but does not express interest in testing whether AI can creatively connect disparate mathematical ideas.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about how much progress AI has made in creatively combining ideas to produce scientific insights.
